title: South Carolina, April 1775 to Cowpens, 17 January 1781
subtitle: Who fought where, who won, and who held the towns and forts: year by year to 1779, then month by month

about: Dates and results come from the South Carolina Archives list of actions (Lipscomb), the National Park Service, the American Battlefield Trust and Wikipedia, each checked against at least one other. Where they disagree, McCrady's History of South Carolina in the Revolution (1901-02), which cites the memoirs and letters of the time, or a commander's own report settles the reading; the others are kept.

A clash is drawn in the colour and shape of the side that won it. A grey diamond is a fight no source scores as a win. A dagger marks a result or a date on which the sources disagree; the pane gives both readings.

Who held each place is reconstructed from the sources named on it, not from a survey of the time; several posts are dated only to the month and marked low. Positions come from markers, park and encyclopedia coordinates, or a place a source describes, each with its precision. 1777 and 1778 are flagged as gaps in the list.

terrain.about: In the United States these tiles come from the USGS's National Elevation Dataset, a survey of the bare ground with no buildings or trees in it. Over the two Carolinas they are read at about 250 m a pixel, so bumps narrower than about 300 m are taken off and the rest smoothed. This is today's ground. The big lakes (Marion, Moultrie, Murray, Wateree, Hartwell, Thurmond and Keowee in South Carolina; Norman, High Rock, Badin, Tillery, Jordan, Falls, Kerr and Gaston further north) are reservoirs of the 20th century: their flat floors are today's water, and in 1775 the rivers ran in their valleys.
terrain.beyond: Beyond the dotted line Mouzon's map stops (north at the Dan, east at 77 W, and the west edge of his South Carolina): only today's relief and sea are drawn there, so the map fills the window.

playback.page_title: South Carolina, 1775 to Cowpens: an orientation

opening.label: Before the first shots
opening.text: South Carolina, early 1775: the royal government still stands. Press play: each year to 1779 comes onto the map at once, with a note on each event, and from 1780 the fights come on month by month, each drawn for the side that won it.

sides.name: British Crown forces (British regulars and Loyalist militia)

events.name: Charleston: arms and powder seized
events.text: Patriot leaders carry off the arms stored in the State House attic and powder from two outlying magazines, without a fight. [T01]

events.name: Fort Charlotte surrenders
events.text: Major James Mayson takes the royal fort on the Savannah River in the Council of Safety's name; the garrison gives it up. [T02]

events.name: Fort Johnson taken
events.text: South Carolina troops under Colonel Isaac Motte walk into Fort Johnson, whose guns the royal navy had just disabled. [T03]

events.name: Ninety Six: Savage's Old Field
events.text: Loyalists surround Major Williamson's Patriot stockade near Ninety Six. Neither side wins; a truce ends the first bloodshed in the state. [T04]

events.name: Great Cane Brake
events.text: Colonel Thomson's rangers and militia surprise a Loyalist camp on the Reedy River and take over a hundred prisoners. [T05]

events.name: Snow Campaign
events.text: Richardson's militia, thousands strong, march through the backcountry; the Loyalist leaders are seized or scattered and snow ends the campaign. [T06]

events.name: Sullivan's Island (Fort Sullivan)
events.text: The unfinished palmetto fort at the harbour mouth drives off the British fleet. [T07]

events.name: Breach Inlet
events.text: Clinton's troops on Long Island find the inlet too deep to wade and cannot cross to Sullivan's Island. [T08]

events.name: Cherokee War begins
events.text: The Cherokee strike the western settlements; the war runs to the treaty of 20 May 1777. [T09]

events.name: Esseneca (Seneca Old Town)
events.text: The Cherokee, with Loyalists under Cameron, ambush Williamson's column at Esseneca before dawn; his men break, Hammond's charge drives the attackers off, and the town is burned. [T10]

events.name: Tamassee and the Ring Fight
events.text: Williamson's men beat a large Cherokee war party (Pickens's Ring Fight near Tamassee) and burn the Lower Towns. [T11]

events.name: Capture of privateers, Charleston
events.text: The only action the Archives list gives for 1778. Neither the list nor any source read says who took which ships. [T12]

events.name: Port Royal Island (Beaufort)
events.text: Moultrie's Continentals and militia beat a British detachment under Major Gardiner near Gray's Hill. [T13]

events.name: Prevost before Charleston
events.text: Prevost's army reaches the Charleston lines, then breaks off and withdraws when it learns Lincoln is hurrying back. [T14]

events.name: Stono Ferry
events.text: Lincoln attacks the British rear guard at the ferry and is repulsed; both sides lose heavily. [T15]

events.name: Monck's Corner
events.text: Tarleton's dragoons surprise Huger's cavalry and militia before dawn, taking horses and wagons and cutting Charleston off. [T17]

events.name: Lenud's Ferry
events.text: Tarleton surprises the American cavalry at the Santee crossing and scatters it. [T18]

events.name: Siege of Charleston
events.text: Clinton's army and fleet besiege the city; on 12 May Lincoln surrenders the army. [T16]

events.name: Waxhaws (Buford's defeat)
events.text: Tarleton's Legion overtakes Buford's Virginians and cuts them down as they try to surrender. [T19]

events.name: Alexander's Old Field (Beckhamville)
events.text: Captain John McClure's Whigs rout a Loyalist muster at Alexander's Old Field (Beckhamville). [T20]

events.name: Huck's Defeat (Williamson's Plantation)
events.text: Patriot militia surprise Captain Huck's Loyalist and British detachment; Huck is killed. [T21]

events.name: Rocky Mount
events.text: Sumter attacks Turnbull's post three times and cannot take it; he withdraws. [T22]

events.name: Hanging Rock I (Davie's raid)
events.text: Davie's North Carolinians ambush a Loyalist party near Hanging Rock and take horses and arms. [T23]

events.name: Hanging Rock II
events.text: Sumter attacks the Loyalist camp at Hanging Rock; heavy losses on both sides, and the Americans leave without holding the post. [T24]

events.name: Cary's Fort (Sumter's raid)
events.text: Sumter's men under Colonel Taylor take Cary's redoubt at Wateree Ferry and a convoy on its way from Ninety Six. [T26]

events.name: Camden
events.text: Cornwallis routs Gates's army north of Camden and takes its guns and wagons. [T25]

events.name: Fishing Creek
events.text: Tarleton surprises Sumter's camp, scatters his command and retakes the convoy and prisoners. [T27]

events.name: Musgrove Mill
events.text: Patriot militia ambush and beat a Loyalist and British force at the Enoree. [T28]

events.name: Nelson's Ferry
events.text: Marion surprises the guard at Sumter's Great Savannah plantation near Nelson's Ferry and frees about 150 Maryland Continentals taken at Camden. [T29]

events.name: Blue Savannah
events.text: Marion ambushes Loyalists at Blue Savannah. Read in Morgan's list, the NPS timeline and the Archives list only. [T30]

events.name: Black Mingo
events.text: Marion attacks a Loyalist camp near midnight and drives it into the swamp. [T31]

events.name: Kings Mountain
events.text: Frontier militia surround and destroy Ferguson's Loyalist force on the ridge. [T32]

events.name: Tearcoat Swamp
events.text: Marion's midnight attack routs Tynes's Loyalist camp. [T33]

events.name: Fish Dam Ford
events.text: Wemyss's night attack on Sumter's camp fails; Wemyss is wounded and taken. [T34]

events.name: Blackstock's
events.text: Tarleton attacks Sumter's position and is beaten back with heavy loss; Sumter is badly wounded. [T35]

events.name: Rugeley's Mill
events.text: Washington's dragoons bluff Colonel Rugeley's Loyalists out of their fortified barn at Clermont with a log painted as a cannon; they surrender without a shot. [T36]

events.name: Halfway Swamp
events.text: Marion meets Major McLeroth's detachment of the 64th Foot; McLeroth answers with a challenge to a fight of twenty picked men, then slips away, and a shot is fired at Singleton's Mill the next day. [T37]

events.name: Hammond's Store
events.text: Washington's dragoons ride down a Loyalist force sent from Georgia. [T38]

events.name: Cowpens
events.text: Morgan defeats Tarleton's British regulars. [T39]

summaries.title: 1775: the Patriots take the forts
summaries.text: The royal government loses its grip. Patriot leaders carry off the arms in Charleston in April, and the Crown's forts at Fort Charlotte (July) and Fort Johnson (September) are taken without a fight. In November Loyalists besiege Williamson's camp at Ninety Six for two days until a truce ends it; in December the Patriots break the Loyalist camp at Great Cane Brake and the Snow Campaign scatters the rest.

summaries.title: 1776: the fort holds, the Cherokee war
summaries.text: In June the palmetto fort on Sullivan's Island drives off the British fleet, and Breach Inlet stops the landing. From July the Cherokee strike the frontier. Williamson's column is ambushed at Esseneca on 1 August, the one Cherokee win drawn here, then beats a war party on 12 August and burns the Lower Towns; Fort Rutledge is built at Esseneca.

summaries.title: 1777: a gap in the list
summaries.text: The Archives list has no action for 1777. The one thing read for the year is the end of the Cherokee war: the treaty of 20 May 1777 gives up the Lower Towns' lands.

summaries.title: 1778: one entry
summaries.text: The list has one entry for the year, the capture of privateers at Charleston on 19 Jun. Nothing read says who took them.

summaries.title: 1779: the war comes south
summaries.text: Moultrie beats Gardiner's detachment on Port Royal Island in February. In May Prevost reaches the Charleston lines and draws off when Lincoln hurries back. On 20 June Lincoln's attack on the rear guard at Stono Ferry is repulsed, and the British fall back to Beaufort. In September Maitland's garrison leaves Beaufort to defend Savannah against the French and Americans, and the town is left to no one.

summaries.title: 1780: Charleston falls, then the partisan war
summaries.text: Clinton lands in February, crosses the Ashley on 29 March, and Lincoln surrenders the city and army on 12 May. Tarleton wins at Monck's Corner, Lenud's Ferry and the Waxhaws, and British posts run inland to Camden, Ninety Six and the Cheraws. The partisans answer: Huck's Defeat, Rocky Mount and Hanging Rock, Sumter's raid at Wateree Ferry, Musgrove Mill and Marion's raids. Gates is routed at Camden on 16 August and Sumter at Fishing Creek two days later. Kings Mountain in October turns the tide; Blackstock's, Rugeley's and Hammond's Store follow.

summaries.title: 1781: Cowpens
summaries.text: Greene's army rests at the Cheraws, and Morgan's detachment works west of the Broad. On 17 January Morgan beats Tarleton at Cowpens. The playback ends here; the later actions are loaded as data for a second stage.

summaries.title: Where things stood on 17 January 1781
summaries.text: The British hold Charleston and its harbour forts, Beaufort, Georgetown, Dorchester, Monck's Corner, Orangeburg, Fort Granby, Fort Galphin, Camden, Ninety Six and Cornwallis's camp at Winnsboro. Greene's army holds the Cheraws. Fort Charlotte, Esseneca, Tamassee and Kingstree are drawn as contested: no source read puts them under either side after June 1780. Who held what is reconstructed from the sources named on each place, not from a survey of the time, and several posts are dated only to the month.

reconstructions.title: The Carolinas, 1775 to 1781: a WarMapper reconstruction
reconstructions.label: 1775 (reconstructed)
reconstructions.about: This is a WarMapper reconstruction, not a period map. Its lines are those of Henry Mouzon's map of the two Carolinas (1775), laid on today's ground: the rivers and the sea coast fitted to today's courses, which they keep, and the main roads and boundary lines carried with them. Mouzon's map was made for the colonies' trade and land grants, not as a survey: his roads are good to a few kilometres, his up-country less. South Carolina is traced at the level of its main lines; North Carolina (since 27 Nov 2026) only for the ground of the campaign of 1781, from Charlotte and Salisbury to Guilford, Hillsborough, Halifax and the Dan. Nothing here has been checked by a historian.
reconstructions.note: Rivers and coast good to about 1-2 km where today's river is in Natural Earth; roads and boundaries to 3-5 km; the far north-west to no better than 10 km. In North Carolina nine towns hold the fit, each found again 1.3-6.6 km from its site when left out. Not yet traced: inlets, islands and sounds, swamps, the lesser roads, ferries and fords; in North Carolina the Neuse, the Tar and the sounds (east of 77 W, beyond the sheet), the rivers and roads of the mountains and of the east, and Mouzon's towns other than those named. Guilford Court House is not on Mouzon's map (it was built in 1774): its name is placed where the battle's playback has it.
reconstructions.credit: WarMapper reconstruction from Mouzon, 1775 (Library of Congress), fitted with Natural Earth; North Carolina checked against Collet, 1770 (Library of Congress)

layers.title: Rivers, as Mouzon draws them (1775), fitted to today's courses
layers.how: Picked by hand every 50-100 pixels of a half-resolution crop and snapped by program to the engraved line; fitted to the ground by matching them to today's rivers (Natural Earth). Rivers with no line in Natural Earth (Pacolet, Tyger, Enoree, Black, Ashley, Combahee), and since the refit of 26 Nov 2026 the Pee Dee, Little Pee Dee and Waccamaw, follow the fit and are low. Each river is one line, joined across the strips where the scan's mounted sections meet (2-6 km). North Carolina (27 Nov 2026): the Catawba and Broad above the 1772 line, the Yadkin to the Pee Dee, the Haw with Reedy Fork and Troublesome Creek, the Deep, the Cape Fear, the Dan and the Roanoke, picked and snapped the same way and matched to Natural Earth (Reedy Fork and Troublesome Creek, which it lacks, follow the fit and are low).

layers.title: The sea coast, as Mouzon draws it, and the sea
layers.how: The outer coast snapped to the engraved line and fitted to today's coast. Inlets, islands and the sounds behind them are not traced yet: the sea is closed across the harbour mouths. North Carolina (27 Nov 2026): the outer coast from Little River past Cape Fear to Bogue, to the sheet's edge at 77 W; the sea is closed across the inlets and the mouth of the Cape Fear.

layers.title: The main roads of 1775, as Mouzon draws them
layers.how: Re-traced 26 Nov 2026: snapped by program to the gap between Mouzon's double lines from end to end and checked by eye; ends joined to the road or town where Mouzon has them meet. Within about 1 km at the towns the fit holds (Camden, Orangeburg, Charles Town, Georgetown, Dorchester, Beaufort, Ninety Six, Long Bluff), about 3-5 km between them. North Carolina (27 Nov 2026): ten roads of the 1781 campaign's ground, snapped the same way: Charlotte and Camden to Salisbury, the Trading Path to Hillsborough, the road by the Quaker meeting houses to Guilford and the Haw, Salem towards the Dan, the Shallow Ford road, Hillsborough to Halifax and north towards the Dan, Salisbury to Oliphant's Mill. Checked against Collet 1770 (S151).

features.name: Cherokee boundary line (1766)
features.basis: Mouzon's line (Mouzon 1775 (S135), Library of Congress g3900.ar139404), picked by hand; the North Carolina lines were fitted to today's state line, which follows them (Natural Earth, S136). Mouzon draws it from the Savannah at a corner tree, past DeWitt's Corner, to a corner tree on the Reedy River and north to the 1772 line. The Cherokee ceded the land east of it in 1766-67 and nearly all the rest in South Carolina at DeWitt's Corner, 20 May 1777, so it is drawn until then.
